meta.title: Who really said "I don't measure a man's success by how high he climbs but how high he bounces when he hits bottom"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Patton's 'bounce when you hit bottom' line rests on a 1979 memoir by Porter B. Williamson; the popular 'how high he climbs' wording is a later rewording.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I don't measure a man's success by how high he climbs but how high he bounces when he hits bottom'?
meta.ogDescription: No Patton speech, letter or diary has this line. It traces to a 1979 recollection by Porter B. Williamson, and the 'how high he climbs' version is a later rewording.

answer.label: Not George S. Patton’s wording — a later paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: No documented source has the popular “how high he climbs” wording. Its core, “Success is how high you bounce when you hit bottom,” is credited to Patton only in Porter B. Williamson’s 1979 book of recollections, I Remember General Patton’s Principles. According to Barry Popik ↗, it has not been found in print during Patton’s lifetime.

source.excerpt: When I fail he tells me, “The test of success is not what you do when you are on top. Success is how high you bounce when you hit bottom.”
trail: Barry Popik’s citation file starts with Porter B. Williamson’s I Remember General Patton’s Principles (1979), p. 9. There Williamson recalls Patton saying, “Success is how high you bounce when you hit bottom.” Popik ↗
Popik notes that the line “has not been found in print in any publication during Patton’s lifetime” and that its authenticity “depends entirely on Williamson’s work.” Popik ↗
The Internet Archive’s catalog record confirms the book: I remember General Patton’s principles, by Porter B. Williamson (Tucson, Ariz.: Management and Systems Consultants, 1979). Internet Archive ↗

Quote Investigator has no entry for the line, and Wikiquote’s George S. Patton page does not list it. Today’s outlets still print the “how high he climbs” version as Patton’s while admitting that a definitive primary source is hard to locate. 19FortyFive ↗
source.excerptNote: Text as transcribed by Barry Popik from Williamson’s 1979 book. It is in the second person and has no “how high he climbs” clause. The “I don’t measure a man’s success” form on quote sites does not appear in this passage.

author.name: George S. Patton
author.heading: About George S. Patton
author.metaLine: 1885–1945 · U.S. Army general, World War II
author.bio: George Smith Patton Jr. was a U.S. Army general. In World War II he commanded the Seventh Army in the Mediterranean, then the Third Army in France and Germany after the Normandy invasion. After he slapped two shell-shocked soldiers in Sicily he was temporarily removed from battlefield command. He returned to lead the Third Army in 1944. Many motivational lines attributed to him come from postwar recollections rather than from his own speeches, letters or diaries.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the popular version
misattribution.intro: Quote sites, military outlets and posters all credit this line to Patton. The documented trail is thinner than that, and the popular wording is not the documented one.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Patton
lead: The line fits the Patton legend well. He was a famously hard-driving general, and his career had a public fall and comeback: he was temporarily removed from battlefield command after the Sicily slapping incidents, then returned to lead the Third Army in 1944 (Wikipedia ↗). That fit helps a resilience slogan travel under his name.

The documented trail starts with one person’s memory. Porter B. Williamson recalled Patton telling him, after a failure, that “the test of success is not what you do when you are on top.” Later books repeated the shorter line, including Fran Tarkenton’s Playing to Win (1985) and Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes (1997). The bigger “I don’t measure a man’s success” form came later (Popik ↗).
context.detailsSummary: Is it possible Patton said something like this?
detailsBody: Yes. A missing wartime printing does not prove he never said it, and Williamson presents it as words Patton spoke to him. But no speech transcript, letter or diary entry has been found, and the polished “how high he climbs” wording is not even in Williamson’s account. The fair summary: the idea is credited to Patton secondhand, and the popular wording is not his documented speech.

sourcesVerified.claim: Williamson's I Remember General Patton's Principles (1979), p. 9, reads: When I fail he tells me, 'The test of success is not what you do when you are on top. Success is how high you bounce when you hit bottom.'
The line has not been found in print in any publication during Patton's lifetime, and its authenticity depends entirely on Williamson's work.

Tarkenton's Playing to Win (1985, p. 59) and Reader's Digest Quotable Quotes (1997, p. 172) print the line. The 1987 Daily News of Los Angeles quotes Smith with the 'bounce after' variant, and the 1988 Rockmart Journal credits Patton with it.
Catalog record: I remember General Patton's principles, by Porter B. Williamson (Tucson, Ariz.: Management and Systems Consultants, 1979).

The popular 'I don't measure a man's success by how high he climbs, but by how high he bounces when he hits bottom' wording is printed as Patton's, and the outlet says a definitive primary source is difficult to locate.
Wikiquote's George S. Patton page does not list the bounce line. Raw wikitext grep for 'bounc', 'hit bottom' and 'test of success' returned no match.

Patton was born 11 November 1885 and died 21 December 1945. He commanded the Seventh and Third Armies, was temporarily removed from battlefield command after the Sicily slapping incidents, and was given the Third Army in 1944.
